seoTitle: How to Delegate Gmail Access in Google Workspace Safely
metaDescription: Learn how to delegate Gmail access in Google Workspace so an assistant or team member can manage your inbox securely without ever needing your password.
intro: Sharing inbox management with an assistant or team member doesn't have to mean handing over a password. Google Workspace has a built-in mail delegation setting that lets one user manage another's Gmail — reading, sending, and organizing mail — while each person keeps their own separate login. The setting is off by default at the domain level, though, so before anyone can delegate access from their own Gmail, an admin has to switch it on for the organization first. This guide walks through exactly where that toggle lives in the Admin Console and what the options next to it actually control.

steps.heading: Get to Gmail's settings inside Google Workspace
steps.body: From the Admin Console, open Apps, then Google Workspace, which expands into a full list of Google services — Calendar, Cloud Search, Drive and Docs, Gmail, Google Chat, and more. Click Gmail to reach its settings rather than looking for delegation under Security or Account, which is where it's easy to assume a permissions setting like this would live.

image.caption: The Apps menu expanded to show every Google Workspace service, with Gmail selected to open its settings.

steps.heading: Find the Mail delegation setting
steps.body: Gmail's User Settings page lists a row of toggles: Mail delegation, Name format, Gmail web offline, Confidential mode, Smart compose personalisation, and others. Mail delegation is described plainly right there: "Let users delegate access to their mailbox to other users in the domain," and by default it shows OFF, applied at the organizational unit you're currently viewing. This is the domain-wide switch — until it's turned on here, individual users won't have the option to add a delegate from their own Gmail settings at all.

image.caption: Gmail's User Settings page with Mail delegation listed as OFF, alongside Name format, Gmail web offline, and Confidential mode.

steps.heading: Turn on delegation and configure what recipients see
steps.body: Clicking to edit Mail delegation expands a checkbox — "Let users delegate access to their mailbox to other users in the domain" — plus a note that any existing delegations will be hidden if you later disable the feature. Below that sits the sender information setting, which controls what a recipient sees when a delegate sends mail on someone else's behalf: either both the account owner and the delegate who actually sent it, or the account owner's name only. There's also a checkbox letting individual users override this display preference themselves rather than being locked to the org-wide default.

image.caption: The expanded Mail delegation panel, with the enable checkbox and the sender-information options that control what recipients see.

steps.heading: Apply the change to the right organizational unit
steps.body: Every setting on this page is scoped to an organizational unit, shown on the left as a tree starting from the top-level domain and branching into any sub-units you've created. Turning on delegation at the top level applies it to everyone; turning it on for a specific unit — say, just an executive team or a support group — limits it to those accounts. Decide the scope before saving, since a domain-wide change affects every mailbox in the organization immediately.

steps.heading: Let the individual user add their delegate
steps.body: Once the admin-level toggle is on, each user adds a delegate from inside their own Gmail — under Settings, the Accounts tab has a "Grant access to your account" section where they enter the delegate's email address. The delegate then gets a confirmation email and, once accepted, can read, send, and organize mail from that inbox using their own Gmail login, with no password ever changing hands.

steps.heading: Understand what delegation does and doesn't allow
steps.body: A delegate can act inside the mailbox — draft and send messages, archive, label, and search — but delegation is not the same as admin access to the account. Delegates can't change the account's password, security settings, or recovery options, and mail sent on someone's behalf is typically labeled as sent by the delegate, depending on how the sender information setting above is configured. That distinction matters for the "give admin access" framing some people search for: delegation shares inbox management, not account control.

faq.question: Can I share my Gmail inbox without giving out my password?
faq.answer: Yes, Gmail delegation lets another user manage your inbox in Google Workspace without ever needing your login credentials, once an admin has enabled delegation for your organization.

faq.question: Who can set up Gmail delegation?
faq.answer: An admin has to turn on the Mail delegation setting in the Admin Console under Apps > Google Workspace > Gmail first; after that, individual users add delegates from their own Gmail settings.

faq.question: What can a delegate actually do in my inbox?
faq.answer: A delegate can read, send, and organize mail, but they can't change the account's password or security settings — delegation shares mailbox management, not full account access.

faq.question: How do I remove someone's delegated access?
faq.answer: The account owner can revoke a delegate from the same Accounts settings in Gmail where they were added; an admin can also disable delegation domain-wide, which hides all existing delegations.

faq.question: What does the sender information setting control?
faq.answer: It decides whether recipients see both the account owner's name and the delegate who actually sent the message, or just the account owner's name alone.
